---
title: "Quiz: marching cubes"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Corner $k$ of a cube has offsets $(x, y, z)$ with $k = x + 2y + 4z$; the case index is $\sum 2^k$ over the corners above $c$.

---

**Q1.** Corners 1, 2 and 4 are above $c$, the others below. What is the case index? How many corners are below?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Add the powers of two.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$2 + 4 + 16 = 22$; five corners are below.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why does marching cubes produce a closed surface, although every cube is processed on its own?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do neighbouring cubes share?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Neighbouring cubes share edges and faces. A crossing point on a shared edge is computed from the same two values, so it is the same point; and if both cubes cut each shared face in the same way (a consistent face rule), their triangles meet edge to edge. The surface can only end where it leaves the volume.
:::

---

**Q3.** How do the 256 cases reduce to 15?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two kinds of symmetry.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The 24 rotations of the cube map a case to another case with the same (rotated) surface: 23 classes. Swapping above and below (complement) gives the same surface with flipped normals: together 15 classes.
:::

---

**Q4.** What is a crack, and how can the 15-case table produce one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of an ambiguous face shared by two cubes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A hole in the surface along a face where the two neighbouring cubes connected the crossing points differently (one separated the bright corners, the other joined them). The 15-case table uses the complement for some cases, which swaps "separate" for "join" on their ambiguous faces; when only one of the two neighbours is complemented, they disagree.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is marching tetrahedra never ambiguous, and what is its price?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the interpolant look like inside a tetrahedron?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Linear interpolation of 4 corner values is an affine function, whose level set is a plane: it cuts a tetrahedron in a single triangle or quadrilateral, and there are no diagonal corners on its (triangular) faces. The price: more triangles (typically 2–4 times), thinner triangles, and a slight dependence on how the cubes were split.
:::

---

**Q6.** A vertex lies on the surface of a bright nucleus where $\nabla I = (0, 0, -12)$. Which way does the outward normal point?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\mathbf n = -\nabla I/\lVert\nabla I\rVert$ for a bright object.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathbf n = (0, 0, 1)$: $I$ decreases towards $+z$, so outside (darker) is in the $+z$ direction.
:::

---

**Q7.** You extract a surface from a binary mask (0/1) at $c = 0.5$ and shade it with gradient normals. Why does it look blocky, and what helps?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the vertices, and which values can the central differences take?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every crossed edge goes from 1 to 0, so every vertex sits at an edge midpoint (terraces), and central differences of 0/1 values point in only a few directions (combinations of $-1, 0, 1$): the normals are blocky too. Blurring the mask slightly before extraction gives grey values that place the vertices and normals smoothly.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Why does the number of triangles grow like $n^2$, while the running time grows like $n^3$, for an $n^3$ volume containing one blob of size proportional to $n$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which cubes produce triangles, and which cubes are visited?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
All $(n-1)^3$ cubes are visited (each in constant time), so the time is $O(n^3)$. Only the cubes the surface passes through produce triangles; their number is proportional to the surface area in voxel units, $\propto n^2$ for a blob whose size grows like $n$.
:::
